primary_sources: Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, Public Law 88-408, August 7, 1964 (paraphrased)
Martin Luther King Jr., "Beyond Vietnam," April 4, 1967 (paraphrased)
John Kerry, testimony to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, April 22, 1971 (paraphrased)
Richard Nixon, address to the nation, November 3, 1969 (paraphrased)

source: original; documents are paraphrases of public sources (see each document's sourcing note); the photograph is a public-domain U.S. Army photograph viewed before writing

stimulus.source_note: DBQ: documents below are the stimulus.

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the Vietnam War changed the relationship between the American people and their government from 1964 to 1975.

documents.title: Power to make war
documents.source: Paraphrase of the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, Public Law 88-408, passed August 7, 1964.
documents.sourcing: Congress is handing the president broad war powers on the strength of his report, so the resolution shows trust in the president at the war's start.
documents.text: Paraphrase of the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, passed August 7, 1964. After reports that North Vietnamese boats had fired on American destroyers, Congress gave President Lyndon Johnson power to take all necessary steps, including the use of armed force, to prevent further aggression in Southeast Asia. The House voted 416 to 0. The Senate voted 88 to 2.

documents.title: Promises shot down
documents.source: Paraphrase of Martin Luther King Jr., "Beyond Vietnam," Riverside Church, New York, April 4, 1967.
documents.sourcing: King is speaking to a church audience as a moral leader, so he frames the war as a drain on the poor at home, not as a military problem.
documents.text: Paraphrase of Martin Luther King Jr., "Beyond Vietnam," April 4, 1967. King said the war was draining money and attention from the poor at home. He said, "The promises of the Great Society have been shot down on the battlefield of Vietnam." His stand against the war broke his close ties with President Johnson.

documents.title: War in the cities
documents.source: Photograph: Cholon district, Saigon, after Tet Offensive operations, 1968. U.S. Army Center of Military History photograph, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
documents.sourcing: An Army photograph of a ruined city district, showing the war as the soldiers and civilians in it endured it.
documents.text: The photograph shows the Cholon district of Saigon after fighting during the Tet Offensive in 1968. Burned-out buildings stand roofless above rubble, and civilians, including children, pick through the wreckage.

documents.title: The silent majority
documents.source: Paraphrase of President Richard Nixon, address to the nation, November 3, 1969.
documents.sourcing: Nixon is speaking to the nation to defend a war many were protesting, so he appeals to citizens he calls the silent majority against the protesters.
documents.text: Paraphrase of President Richard Nixon, address to the nation, November 3, 1969. Nixon said a silent majority of Americans supported his plan to end the war with honor. He asked them to stand with him against a vocal minority that demanded immediate withdrawal, and warned that a hasty American defeat would betray the men who had fought.

documents.title: A veteran speaks
documents.source: Paraphrase of John Kerry, testimony to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, April 22, 1971.
documents.sourcing: Kerry speaks as a decorated veteran for other veterans, so his criticism carries the weight of firsthand service rather than outside opinion.
documents.text: Paraphrase of John Kerry, testimony to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, April 22, 1971. Kerry said the war was a civil war by a people seeking freedom from any colonial influence. Most Vietnamese, he said, did not know the difference between communism and democracy; they wanted to work in their rice paddies in peace, and to be left alone.

documents.title: Two stories
documents.source: Paraphrase of the Pentagon Papers, a secret Defense Department study published in 1971.
documents.sourcing: The study was a secret government record, not a public speech, so it shows what officials knew in private against what they told the public.
documents.text: Paraphrase of the Pentagon Papers, published in 1971. The secret Defense Department study showed a pattern of official deception: leaders had told the public the war was going well while their own reports said otherwise. Daniel Ellsberg, a Pentagon official, leaked the study to the press.

documents.title: Congress answers back
documents.source: Paraphrase of the War Powers Resolution, passed November 7, 1973, over President Nixon's veto.
documents.sourcing: Congress is writing a law to limit the president, so the resolution shows the legislature reclaiming power it had given away in 1964.
documents.text: Paraphrase of the War Powers Resolution, November 1973. Congress passed the resolution over President Nixon's veto. It requires the president to report troop deployments to Congress within 48 hours, and lets Congress force troops home after 60 days. Congress acted because presidents had waged a long war and widened it without a declaration of war.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the Vietnam War changed the relationship between the American people and their government from 1964 to 1975, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of the change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the Cold War policy of containment, the domino theory, or the United States emerging from World War II as a world power.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument, or background from a later century, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant content from at least three documents, such as the Tonkin Resolution, King's speech, and the Tet photograph.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting or naming documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument, including the Pentagon Papers and the War Powers Resolution.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example outside the documents, such as the My Lai massacre, the Kent State shootings, or the Twenty-Sixth Amendment.
rubric.notEarned: Naming an outside example with no specific detail, or repeating a document's content, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation for at least two documents, such as Kerry speaking as a veteran or the Pentagon Papers showing private knowledge against public claims.
rubric.notEarned: Restating a document's sourcing note without explaining why it matters does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the thesis by showing that trust broke down and yet a large part of the public kept supporting the war, or weighing change against continuity in the presidency's power.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The Vietnam War changed the relationship between the American people and their government to a great extent, turning the broad trust of 1964 into open distrust by the early 1970s, though the change was uneven, since a large part of the public kept backing the war and the presidency kept much of its power.
Context: The United States entered the 1960s as the leader of the non-Communist world, committed to containment and the domino theory, with a public that broadly trusted its government.
Evidence: Document 1 shows Congress handing Johnson war powers almost unanimously in 1964. Document 2 shows King arguing the war drained the Great Society. Document 3 shows the war reaching Saigon's cities at Tet. Document 4 shows Nixon appealing to a silent majority against protesters. Document 5 shows a veteran telling the Senate the war was a mistake. Document 6 shows officials saying one thing in public and another in private. Document 7 shows Congress passing a law to limit the president.
Outside evidence: The My Lai massacre and its cover-up, the killing of four students at Kent State in 1970, and the Twenty-Sixth Amendment lowering the voting age to 18 in 1971 all show the same break in trust.
Complexity: Trust broke down, but not evenly: Nixon won reelection in 1972, and the War Powers Resolution limited the president on paper while leaving him the commander in chief, so the change was real and partial at once.
